name: Data from: Integrative discovery and functional dependency mapping uncover essential chimeric RNAs in the active transcriptome
description: Chimeric RNAs are a diverse class of molecules defined as RNA transcripts containing genetic information for multiple genes that arise from both DNA-level and RNA-level fusion events. While their expression patterns across various tissue types and disease states have been well-documented, the biological function of these transcripts remains poorly understood. In this study, we developed an integrative prediction pipeline to establish a comprehensive atlas of 569,640 chimeric RNAs across 1,019 cancer cell lines, providing the high-resolution landscape required for functional interrogation. name: Genomic Entropy confers an aggressive Phenotype in Mesothelioma
description: This draft repository contains supplementary data described in the draft manuscript - Genomic Entropy confers an aggressive Phenotype in Mesothelioma, manuscript in presubmission stage. The data includes somatic mutations (text files) obtained from whole-exome sequence analysis of 277 mesotheliomas and analysed using phylogenetic methods to infer the genetic evolution of mesothelioma. This repo also includes code description of the software used, statistical results and a README file that describes the content of each file.

name: Therapeutic Inhibition of HDAC10 Confers Therapeutic Vulnerability on Leukemia Stem Cell–like Cells Resistant to the Venetoclax + Azacitidine Regimen in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
description: Although the venetoclax + azacitidine (VA) combination regimen is highly effective for elderly and other acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients unsuitable for intensive chemotherapy (IC), the treatment is limited by prolonged myelosuppression and eventual relapse and resistance. Through high-throughput sequencing, we found that histone deacetylase 10 (HDAC10) was aberrantly upregulated in VA-resistant leukemia stem cell (LSC)–like cells. Overexpression (OE) of HDAC10 in LSC-like cells reduced their sensitivity to VA treatment. Both short-hairpin ribonucleic acid (shRNA)–mediated knockdown (KD) and pharmacological inhibition of HDAC10 significantly reversed LSC resistance by enhancing F-box/WD repeat–containing protein 7 (FBXW7) acetylation and upregulating FBXW7 protein levels, which in turn suppressed induced myeloid leukemia cell differentiation protein (MCL-1) expression and overcame LSC-driven resistance to the VA regimen. Furthermore, elevated FBXW7 enhanced ubiquitination of HDAC10 at the lysine 355 (Lys355) site, leading to further HDAC10 degradation. Functionally, administration of chidamide into VA-resistant patient-derived tumor xenograft (PDX) models mitigated leukemia blasts and significantly prolonged survival in these models. Finally, in 13 high-risk VA-refractory AML patients, adding chidamide to venetoclax + azacitidine (VAC) yielded a composite complete-remission (CR) rate of 38.5% and a 1‑year overall-survival (OS) rate of 52.7% with manageable toxicity, demonstrating potential benefits for patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) AML. In summary, this study identified a new vulnerable therapeutic target in the treatment of resistant acute R/R AML.

name: RNA-seq of Caki-1 clear cell renal cell carcinoma cells with VGLL4 overexpression versus wild-type controls
description: Vestigial-like family member 4 (VGLL4) is implicated in tumor suppression in multiple cancers, but its downstream transcriptomic effects in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) remain incompletely defined. In this study, we performed mRNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to profile transcriptional changes induced by VGLL4 overexpression in the human ccRCC cell line Caki-1. VGLL4-overexpressing cells and wild-type controls were analyzed with three independent biological replicates per group (n = 3 per group; total n = 6). Paired-end sequencing (2 × 150 bp) was conducted on an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus platform. Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction; genes with |log2FoldChange| > 1 and FDR-adjusted q-value < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. Processed data files include gene-level read count and FPKM expression matrices, as well as differential expression results.

name: Inhibition of 3-mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase enhances CD8+ T-cell antitumor immunity
description: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a redox-active gasotransmitter implicated in tumor progression and immune regulation. The enzyme 3-mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase (3-MST) is a key contributor to endogenous H2S and polysulfide production, but its role in tumor–immune interactions remains poorly defined. Here, we show that 3-MST is the most abundantly expressed H2S-synthesizing enzyme in human renal cell carcinoma cells (RCC) and that high 3-MST expression correlates with reduced patient survival. Pharmacological inhibition of 3-MST lowered intracellular H2S levels in Renca renal carcinoma cells, suppressed proliferation, induced apoptosis, disrupted cellular metabolism, and increased expression of immune-related genes and proteins. In immune cells, partial inhibition of 3-MST promoted T cell activation, as evidenced by increased CD69 expression on CD3+, CD4+, and CD8+ T cells. In contrast, complete inhibition of 3-MST, achieved by high concentrations of the inhibitor, modestly reduced CD8+ T cell proliferation. Functionally, 3-MST inhibition potentiated antigen-specific CD8+ T cell-mediated killing of tumor cells, an effect further amplified by PD-L1 blockade. These results establish 3-MST as a redox-sensitive metabolic driver of tumor growth and immune evasion in RCC and demonstrate that its inhibition can boost antitumor immune responses, offering a potential avenue for combination immunotherapy. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.redox.2026.104373

name: Comparative Analysis of Primary and Liver Fibroblasts Reveals MET as a Potent Target in Pancreatic Cancer Metastasis [scRNA-Seq]
description: The tumor microenvironment drives many malignant features of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). The fibroblasts within pancreatic tumors promote tissue remodeling, immune suppression, and resistance to therapy. However, the interactions between stromal populations and pancreatic cancer cells are less understood in the liver, the most frequent site of PDAC metastasis. To address this, we employ single cell transcriptomics to compare primary pancreatic vs. liver PDAC lesions. Using a ligand-receptor interaction tool, we assess upregulated pathways in liver PDAC. Here, we identify the expression of hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) in fibroblasts and its receptor MET in cancer cells are both markedly increased in the PDAC liver niche. Using functional assays, we validate that mitogenic MET signaling is activated in PDAC cells by liver-derived fibroblasts. Importantly, the inhibition of MET signaling leads to reduced tumor growth in immune competent mouse models. Collectively, our data demonstrates that liver stromal-epithelial crosstalk networks engage in signaling pathways distinct from primary pancreatic tumors, highlighting opportunities to develop new treatments for metastatic disease.

name: Single cell transcriptomic atlas of patient bone marrow biopsies after anti-BCMA CAR T cell therapy [scRNA-Seq]
description: CAR-T cell therapy is an effective treatment for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. However, this treatment has been linked to a number of potentially fatal adverse events with incompletely understood biological underpinnings. These events include a failure of bone marrow (BM) regeneration, which leads to dysfunctional hematopoiesis, a condition also referred to as immune effector cell-associated hematotoxicity (ICAHT). To address this issue, we analyzed BM core biopsies of CAR-T cell treated patients (N=24) by combining single-cell RNA-sequencing with single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomics. Focusing on patients with ICAHT (N=10), our analysis revealed hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niche alterations towards a cellular network around inflamed mesenchymal cells that relay IFN- signaling from T cells to monocytes. Monocytes in turn provide pro-inflammatory feedback to mesenchymal cells through IL1B signaling. HSCs from cytopenic patients exposed to this niche up-regulate a senescence signature, indicating a cause of dysfunctional hematopoiesis. Our study deciphers a BM niche interaction network that maintains prolonged inflammation and impairs bone marrow regeneration by inducing HSC senescence.

name: Spatial transcriptomic atlas of patient bone marrow biopsies after anti-BCMA CAR T cell therapy [Xenium]
description: Anti-BCMA CAR-T cell therapy is an efficient treatment strategy for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Nevertheless, a set of potentially fatal adverse events has been linked to this treatment, including immune effector cell-associated hematotoxicity (ICAHT), a condition with largely unknown biological underpinnings. To address this issue, we analyzed bone marrow (BM) core biopsies of anti-BCMA CAR-T cell treated patients at spatial single-cell resolution by combining single-cell RNA-sequencing with spatial transcriptomics by in situ sequencing. Focusing on patients with sustained ICAHT, our integrated analysis strategy revealed an inflammatory mesenchymal cell population, serving as the signaling hub to relay inflammatory signaling to monocytes within the BM, which we validated in vitro. HSCs from cytopenic patients up-regulated a senescence signature, indicating a putative cause of perturbed hematopoiesis. Our study deciphers a mechanism to maintain prolonged inflammation of the BM microenvironment and suggests that this inflammatory state may underlie ICAHT by inducing HSC senescence.

name: PLA2G2E is an inducer of IL-1B and CXCL2
description: The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) limits the efficacy of antitumor immune responses. Myeloid cells within the TME are thought to be educated to establish this immunosuppressive milieu, although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that tumor cells reprogram myeloid cells to produce interleukin-1B (IL-1B) and CXC chemokine ligand 2 (CXCL2) through the phospholipase PLA2G2E. IL-1B and CXCL2 in turn fuel the immunosuppressive TME by recruiting myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Targeting PLA2G2E promotes tumor clearance in mice. Together, these findings identify PLA2G2E as a mediator of tumor cell-myeloid cell communication and define the major sources of IL-1B and CXCL2 in the TME, highlighting PLA2G2E as a potential therapeutic target in cancer.

name: Genetic and biochemical screens identify MGAT1 as a druggable glycosyltransferase target in STK11-mutant lung cancer
description: Checkpoint inhibitors are standard-of-care therapies for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but their efficacy is limited in tumors with STK11 mutations, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. Here, we performed complementary in vivo and in vitro CRISPR-Cas9 functional genomic screens to identify genes whose loss restores sensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy. We found that loss of MGAT1, a Golgi glycosyltransferase critical for the maturation of high-mannose N-glycans into hybrid and complex glycan structures, reversed resistance to anti-PD-1 treatment in syngeneic mouse tumor models harboring STK11 mutations. Parallel co-culture screens with antigen-matched CD8+ T cells further showed that disruption of N-glycosylation strongly sensitized tumor cells to T cell-mediated killing. Genetic rescue studies demonstrated that this immune-evasion phenotype depends on MGAT1 catalytic activity, supporting direct biochemical interrogation of the enzyme. Using purified human MGAT1 and a UDP-Glo™ glycosyltransferase assay, we established a tractable screening platform and performed a 500,000-compound biochemical high-throughput screen, identifying an initial hit (compound 1; IC50 = 197 μM). Subsequent medicinal chemistry optimization delivered progressively more potent analogs, including TNG-9333 (0.814 μM) and TNG-2673 (0.043 μM) and represented a >1000-fold improvement in biochemical potency from the starting hit. Crystal structures of human MGAT1 in apo, UDP-bound, UDP-GlcNAc-bound, and inhibitor-bound states, together with SPR and DSF analyses, revealed that this chemical series engages a previously unrecognized allosteric pocket and inhibits MGAT1 through a UDP-noncompetitive mechanism. Collectively, our work implicates N-glycosylation as a key mediator of immune evasion and establishes MGAT1 as a ligandable, structurally tractable target for small-molecule drug discovery.

name: SMC5/6 safeguards chromatin compartments and TAD boundaries for genome stability
description: SMC5/6, a member of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes family, coordinates 3D genome organization, chromatin states, and transcriptional regulation, yet its role in higher-order chromatin architecture remains poorly defined. Here, we investigate the impact of conditional SMC5 depletion in human B lymphoblastoid cells. Hi-C analyses reveal global rewiring of chromatin interactions, with increased long-range and reduced short-range contacts, leading to altered large-scale chromosome organization. SMC5 loss induces changes in 3D genome compartmentalization affecting ~2% of the genome and is accompanied by transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory and cancer-associated gene programs. SMC5 depletion also promotes double-strand break accumulation, preferentially in active compartments and following transcriptional level of genes. However, regions undergoing architectural reorganization display comparatively fewer breaks, indicating that chromatin changes are not driven by DNA damage. Together, our findings establish SMC5/6 as a key regulator of chromatin compartmentalization and TAD boundary integrity, linking 3D genome organization to transcriptional control and genome stability. name: Roles of SMC5/6 in chromatin state maintenance and TAD insulation impacting genome integrity [ChIP-Seq]
description: SMC5/6, one of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) complexes, facilitates different DNA transactions, but its role in chromatin architecture remains largely unknown. Here, we explored the impact of SMC5 conditional depletion in a human B cell lymphoblastoid cell line model. Using Hi-C, we found that SMC5 loss results in significant compartment changes affecting 2% of the genome. This leads to prominent upregulation of inflammatory and cancer-related genes present in repressed chromatin states and expression of early replication fragility. SMC5/6 loss increases long-range chromatin contacts and decreases short-range contacts, resulting in unique chromosome arm patterns. SMC5 depletion leads to accumulation of double-strand breaks (DSBs) in active compartments but not at differential TAD borders, indicating that its role in modulating genome architecture is not directly linked with DSB accumulation. These findings underscore the pivotal roles of SMC5/6 in preserving chromatin states and TAD boundary integrity for genome stability.

name: Nemo-like kinase limits T cell activation while preserving anti-tumor responses
description: T cell dysfunction limits the efficacy of cancer immunity, yet the molecular checkpoints that preserve T cell function within the tumor microenvironment are not fully understood. In this study, we identify a previously unrecognized, T cell–intrinsic role for Nemo-like kinase (NLK) as a critical mediator of sustained anti-tumor responses. In our experiments, NLK emerged as a dual-function modulator: Although NLK deficiency in CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells increases proliferation and cytokine production in vitro via enhanced NFAT and AP-1 activation, its loss in vivo paradoxically impairs tumor control. In murine tumor models, NLK-deficient tumor-infiltrating T cells exhibit blunted effector activity resulting in accelerated tumor progression. Conversely, human CAR T cells that overexpress NLK demonstrate superior killing capacity towards target tumor cells. These findings establish NLK as an essential early brake on T cell activation while protecting against their chronic dysfunction, and reveal a molecular pathway that sustains anti-tumor immunity.

name: Cytosolic RNA-DNA hybrid detection by cytoDRIP-seq in Rrn3 KD RAW264.7 cells
description: Innate immune responses are known to detect both self- and non-self-derived nucleic acids. Recent studies have reported that cytosolic RNA–DNA hybrids derived from R-loops generated under transcriptional stress can activate innate immune signaling; however, the underlying mechanisms and physiological significance remain largely unclear. In this study, we found that nucleolar stress, induced by loss of the nucleolar protein RRN3 and related perturbations, leads to the cytosolic accumulation of RNA–DNA hybrids derived from ribosomal DNA loci (hereafter referred to as ribo-RNA–DNA hybrids). These ribo-RNA–DNA hybrids are processed in an XPA/XPC/XPF/XPG-dependent manner and partially activate both the cGAS–STING and TLR3–TICAM-1 pathways. Notably, their presence alone does not trigger overt inflammatory responses but instead establishes a primed state, resulting in markedly enhanced responses to subsequent secondary stimulation. We further observed that this phenomenon is also present in pathological contexts, including Diamond–Blackfan anemia and tumor cells. Based on these findings, the present study aims to further characterize cytosolic RNA–DNA hybrids generated under nucleolar stress. To this end, we constructed next-generation sequencing libraries from immunoprecipitation-enriched cytosolic RNA–DNA hybrids and performed sequencing analyses to define their global sequence features.

name: An Epigenetic–Apoptotic Axis Governs the Generation of Focal Extrachromosomal and Integrated MYC amplifications
description: Extrachromosomal (ecDNA) and inherited DNA amplifications are frequent drivers of tumor evolution, yet the mechanisms governing site-specific oncogenic copy gains remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that increased expression of the histone 3 lysine 9, 36 (H3K9/36) tri-demethylase KDM4C or loss or inhibition of the H3K36 tri-methyltransferase SETD2 directly promotes focal MYC amplification in non-transformed and transformed human cells. These same epigenetic alterations are associated with MYC copy gains across multiple human tumor datasets. Disruption of apoptotic surveillance or loss of TP53 accelerates the emergence of both MYC ecDNAs and inherited amplifications that are driven by epigenetic perturbation and is accompanied by enhanced clonogenic growth. Genetic depletion or pharmacologic inhibition of KDM4C partially or completely suppresses MYC amplification in vitro and in vivo. These findings collectively define a chromatin–apoptotic axis that drives focal ecDNAs and inherited MYC amplifications, while identifying biomarkers and therapeutic targets to constrain tumors with MYC-amplification.

name: Transcriptomic changes in HUVEC with PDL1 knockdown
description: Programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an immune checkpoint protein expressed in vascular endothelial cells (ECs). In contrast to cancer, our understanding of endothelial PD-L1 in relation to metabolic syndromes and its vascular complications is less studied. For example, its regulation and intrinsic function remain unclear. Here, we show endothelial PD-L1 is regulated by leptin receptor signaling. In particular, endothelial PD-L1 expression is likely affected by leptin resistance. A lack of leptin receptors leads to PD-L1 downregulation in vascular ECs via post-translational degradation. To understand the fundamental roles of endothelial PD-L1, RNA interference and selective knockout are employed in human endothelium and animals, respectively. Silencing or deleting endothelial PD-L1 expression delays the cycle progression and proliferation, because of Ras/MAPK inactivation. During obesity, endothelial PD-L1 deficiency impairs the EC turnover and worsened the vascular function. Overall, we provide a new insight of how endothelial PD-L1 contributes to vascular homeostasis, suggesting its pathophysiological importance in maintaining cellular turnover.

name: Roles of SMC5/6 in chromatin state maintenance and TAD insulation impacting genome integrity [HiC]
description: SMC5/6, one of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) complexes, facilitates different DNA transactions, but its role in chromatin architecture remains largely unknown. Here, we explored the impact of SMC5 conditional depletion in a human B cell lymphoblastoid cell line model. Using Hi-C, we found that SMC5 loss results in significant compartment changes affecting 2% of the genome. This leads to prominent upregulation of inflammatory and cancer-related genes present in repressed chromatin states and expression of early replication fragility. SMC5/6 loss increases long-range chromatin contacts and decreases short-range contacts, resulting in unique chromosome arm patterns. SMC5 depletion leads to accumulation of double-strand breaks (DSBs) in active compartments but not at differential TAD borders, indicating that its role in modulating genome architecture is not directly linked with DSB accumulation. These findings underscore the pivotal roles of SMC5/6 in preserving chromatin states and TAD boundary integrity for genome stability.

name: Shared molecular regulation of quiescence in neural and glioma stem cells reveals therapeutic vulnerabilities
description: Quiescent glioma cells evade chemoradiation and drive glioblastoma recurrence by reactivating to repopulate the tumour, but are hard to study due to their rarity and difficulty maintaining quiescence in vitro. We hypothesised that quiescence programs conserved between neural stem cells and glioma cells could be exploited to lock glioma cells in quiescence and prevent reactivation. Using single-cell RNA-sequencing and patient-derived glioma stem cell lines, we found that although glioma cells resist entering deep quiescence, they share conserved activation trajectories with neural stem cells. Because this conservation lets a tractable neural progenitor line act as a surrogate for rare quiescent glioma cells, we queried LINCS L1000 signatures across more than 3,000 compounds and validated the top classes (mTOR, ATPase and histone lysine methyltransferase inhibitors) as quiescence promoters in glioma stem cell lines. By establishing conserved activation programs and enabling cross-cell-type screening, our work provides a strategy for driving therapy-resistant glioma cells into quiescence.

name: Functional genetic screening identifies ITGA3 as a regulator of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma growth and organoid architecture
description: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the deadliest cancers, with limited therapeutic options. In this study, we performed a targeted CRISPR screen and identified integrin a3 (ITGA3) as a dependency. ITGA3 knockdown resulted in reduced organoid cell viability, loss of luminal structure, and decreased invasion in collagen I. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that ITGA3 knockdown resulted in upregulation of cilia-related pathways, a finding not previously reported. ITGA3 knockdown also reduced tumor growth in vivo. This study expands on the role of ITGA3 in promoting aggressive cancer phenotypes and provides a novel link to cilia-related transcriptional programs.

name: Studying the role of humanized-TLR8 on immune cell dynamics in the placental microenvironment in a spontaneous mouse model of aPL-induced pregnancy loss
description: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) patients have a high risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes, especially if they have anti-phospholipid (APL) autoantibodies. While human TLR8 (huTLR8) has been implicated in APL antibody-mediated trophoblast injury in vitro, its in vivo role in pregnancy is unexplored. We report a novel mouse model of pregnancy loss in SLE-prone mice expressing huTLR8. Placental analysis revealed early developmental defects starting post-implantation, including de-differentiation of decidual stromal cells (DSCs) a thin junctional zone, impaired vascularization, infarcts, and inflammation. Profound immune dysregulation was evident at E8.5 including increased myeloid cells and CD8 T cells and decreased uterine natural killer (uNK) cells. RNA sequencing revealed downregulated pregnancy-specific glycoproteins, reduced uNK cell-associated genes, and an upregulated myeloid cell signature. Bone marrow chimeras demonstrated preferential activation of huTLR8-expressing placental Ly6C+ monocytes. Spatial transcriptomics at E9.5 confirmed uNK cell loss, decreased IL15 expression by DSCs and myeloid cells, and inflammatory aggregates containing myeloid cells and IFN?-expressing CD8 T cells in the maternal layers. We propose that huTLR8, through myeloid cell activation and cytolytic T cell recruitment, contributes to autoantibody-associated placental injury in SLE. This model provides a valuable platform to dissect early pathogenic events in SLE-associated pregnancy loss and identify new therapeutic targets.

name: Modular engineered colorectal tumor microenvironments for immuno-oncology research and drug development
description: The development of cancer immunotherapies is hindered by the lack of human-relevant models that accurately translate to patient outcomes. We combine patient-derived colorectal tumor organoids (PDOs) and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) into floating extracellular matrix drops to form miniature colorectal tumors. These SHaking Organoid COcultures (SHOCOs) reproducibly capture key features of the tumor microenvironment (TME), including physiologically relevant ECM, hypoxic regions, and a diversified stromal compartment that captures primary CAF states. Compared with traditional PDO-based co-culture models, SHOCOs maintain immune cells in numbers, states and functional interactions that more closely reflect the physiological tumor microenvironment. The modularity of the system allowed controlled simulation of diverse patient tumor archetypes, and defining how TME components shape therapy response. Immune-rich SHOCOs treated with T-cell bispecific antibodies exhibited robust anti-tumor responses that were stronger and more rapid than their PDO-based counterparts. Stroma-rich tumors, on the other hand, diminished therapy responses by physically hindering both immune cell recruitment and limiting antibody penetration. Thus, SHOCOs enable the construction of hypothesis-driven tumor microenvironments, providing a versatile platform to dissect immune and stromal tumor biology and to catalyze the discovery of novel therapeutic approaches.

name: Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics Across Populations With Perianal Fistulizing Crohn’s Disease Shows Proinflammatory CD4+ Macrophage Involvement in Disease Progression
description: Background and aims: Perianal fistulizing Crohn’s disease (CD) is a severe complication associated with altered immune and tissue responses. This study aimed to identify cellular and molecular features distinguishing inflamed rectal CD with and without fistula across African American (AA) and European American (EA) populations. Results: Single-cell sequencing of 262,000 rectal mucosal cells revealed reduced phagocytic and antigen-processing signatures in CD4⁺CD68⁺ macrophages from fistulizing CD. These macrophages formed large aggregates near epithelial crypts and altered local cellular signaling networks. The strongest cellular pathway differences occurred between AA and EA patients with fistulizing disease and between fistulizing and non-fistulizing CD among AA patients. Conclusion: CD4⁺ macrophage aggregation and altered immune-cell interactions may contribute to the severe inflammation underlying perianal fistula formation and progression, with population-specific differences potentially influencing disease severity.

name: MAPK signaling links BRD2 chromatin occupancy to PI3K/AKT inhibitor sensitivity [ChIP-Seq]
description: Bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) proteins, BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, and BRDT, are acetyl-lysine readers that couple histone acetylation to transcriptional output by recruiting elongation and transcription factor complexes to chromatin. BET proteins are promising therapeutic targets, but the functions of individual family members remain incompletely understood. Here we identify BRD2 as a co-targetable vulnerability with PI3K/AKT inhibition in breast cancer. Pan-BET inhibition and BRD2 knockout each synergized with PI3K pathway inhibitors in breast cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and in vivo. BRD2 knockout impaired proliferation of triple-negative breast cancer cells and transcriptionally upregulated key signaling and stress response pathways, including the DNA damage response. Mechanistically, BRD2 is phosphorylated at Serine 37 (Ser37) by the mitogen- and stress-activated kinases MSK and RSK, and Ser37 phosphorylation is required for BRD2 chromatin binding and reader function. Together, these findings identify BRD2 as a phosphorylation-dependent, co-targetable vulnerability in PI3K pathway-inhibited breast cancer.

name: RNA-seq data from glioblastoma organ chips interpret the immunosuppressive effect of PILRA
description: To investigate the role of PILRα in glioblastoma (GBM) immune evasion, we established a humanized multicellular GBM–blood–brain barrier (BBB) organ-on-a-chip microfluidic model. The chip integrates a 3D tumor compartment composed of U-87 MG glioma cells, human cortical neurons, and brain fibroblasts, with perfusable vascular channels lined with brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMECs) that form a functional BBB under physiological shear stress. A recirculating immune cell perfusion system incorporating primary human CD8⁺ T cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), and dendritic cells was introduced to reconstitute the tumor–immune–BBB interface. This platform recapitulates progressive BBB breakdown, immune cell trafficking, and tumor invasion dynamics. To investigate PILRα-mediated transcriptional reprogramming, we performed bulk RNA-sequencing on organ-on-a-chip cultures from control (NC) and PILRA-overexpressing (OE-PILRA) groups.

name: Opposing effects of Lrig1 and Lrig3 on EGFR signaling maintain intestinal homeostasis and mitigate the likelihood of colonic neoplasia
description: This study investigates how LRIG1 and LRIG3 exert opposing control over EGFR signaling to maintain intestinal stem-cell (ISC) homeostasis and suppress tumor formation. LRIG1 is an established negative regulator of ERBB/EGFR signaling and tumor suppressor, whereas the function of LRIG3 in the intestine has been less clear. Using conditional mouse models that delete Lrig3 in Lrig1-expressing cells, the authors show that loss of LRIG3 in an LRIG1-null background produces the opposite signaling effect of LRIG1 loss: EGFR/ERBB, ERK, and WNT signaling are markedly reduced. This signaling imbalance causes loss of ISC identity and proliferation, increased cell death and crypt disruption, and a striking shift of stem cells toward immature secretory states, including Paneth/goblet intermediate cells in the small intestine and REG4⁺ deep secretory/goblet cells in the colon; single-cell RNA-seq further reveals reduced stem-cell programs together with activation of injury-responsive reserve/persister stem-cell programs. Importantly, the biological consequence extends to tumorigenesis: whereas Lrig1CreER/+; Apcfl/+ mice develop highly dysplastic distal colonic tumors, deletion of only one Lrig3 allele substantially reduces EGFR/WNT signaling and can abrogate tumor formation. Collectively, the paper proposes that LRIG1 restrains while LRIG3 supports EGFR signaling, and the antagonistic balance between these proteins establishes the signaling range required for ISC maintenance, appropriate lineage differentiation, intestinal crypt homeostasis, and protection against colonic neoplasia.

name: HER2-Targeted ADC Impairs Lysosomal Maturation and Triggers Autophagic Degradation of YAP to Abrogate Stemness and Progression in Advanced HNSCC
description: RC48 is a HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate that exerts its antitumor activity in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma through multiple synergistic mechanisms: In vitro experiments demonstrated that RC48 dose-dependently inhibits cell proliferation, induces G2/M phase arrest, and promotes apoptosis, while simultaneously downregulating the anti-apoptotic proteins BCL-2/MCL-1 and the cyclin-dependent kinase CDK4/pRb; Mechanistically, RC48 promotes YAP nuclear translocation via the non-classical Hippo pathway but inhibits its downstream stemness factors c-MYC and SOX2; furthermore, it induces increased lysosomal membrane permeability, leading to the release of cathepsins CTSB/CTSL, which subsequently cleave and degrade the YAP protein—a process that does not rely on the proteasome pathway. YAP exhibits high-frequency overexpression in clinical head and neck squamous cell carcinoma samples (positive rate: 98.41%), and both gene silencing of YAP or the use of the small-molecule inhibitor verteporfin can significantly enhance RC48's antiproliferative, pro-apoptotic, and anti-migratory/invasive effects; In patient-derived organoids, CDX, and PDX models, the combination of RC48 with verteporfin demonstrates a significantly superior synergistic antitumor effect compared to monotherapy, accompanied by inhibition of proliferation, enhanced DNA damage, and reduced expression of stemness markers, without inducing significant toxicity at therapeutic doses. This study provides a systematic experimental basis for the clinical translation of the RC48–YAP blockade strategy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.

name: Redundant functions of TBX2 and TBX3 control urothelial stratification and lineage stability during bladder development
description: Background The urothelium is a specialized stratified epithelium that forms the permeability barrier of the urinary bladder and consists of basal, intermediate, and superficial cell layers. Although the closely related T-box transcription factors genes TBX2 and TBX3 are implicated in bladder cancer, their functions during normal urothelial development remain unknown. Methods We analyzed Tbx2/TBX2 and Tbx3/TBX3 expression during murine bladder development using RNA in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence. The individual and combined functions of Tbx2 and Tbx3 in urothelial development were examined using conditional gene targeting in mice. Cellular consequences of Tbx2/Tbx3 loss were assessed by marker analysis across developmental stages and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of late fetal bladders. Transcriptomic profiling of isolated mutant urothelial cells was used to identify gene programs associated with loss of Tbx2/Tbx3, and developmental signaling pathways were analyzed by expression profiling of pathway components and targets. Results Tbx2/TBX2 and Tbx3/TBX3 were continuously co-expressed in the developing murine urothelium. Individual loss of either gene had little effect on urothelial architecture, whereas combined loss disrupted stratification and resulted in a monolayered epithelium predominantly composed of superficial cell-like cells. These defects were preceded by reduced expression of ΔNP63, a key regulator of urothelial stratification and basal/intermediate cell differentiation, activation of mesenchymal gene programs, and altered BMP and TGFβ pathway activity in the developing epithelium. Conclusion TBX2 and TBX3 are redundant developmental regulators of urothelial stratification and differentiation. By maintaining epithelial identity and preventing inappropriate activation of mesenchymal programs, these factors establish a developmental framework relevant to understanding epithelial plasticity in bladder disease.

name: A Syngeneic Murine Glioma Model Recapitulates Key Molecular, Immunologic, and Functional Features of Human Glioblastoma Enabling Therapeutic Development
description: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of effective therapies. Here, we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-γ (mIFN-γ) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

name: CCDC69 Functions as a Tumor Suppressor in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
description: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype of breast cancer with limited treatment options. To investigate the biological role of coiled-coil domain-containing protein 69 (CCDC69) in TNBC, transcriptome sequencing was performed in TNBC cells with CCDC69 overexpression or knockdown and their corresponding control cells. Differential gene expression analysis and pathway enrichment analysis were conducted to identify signaling pathways associated with CCDC69. name: Modeling the active proteome by context-matched perturbation signatures
description: Measuring protein activity on a global scale remains a central challenge in molecular biology. We hypothesized that the functional contribution of proteins to cellular processes can be inferred from perturbation-induced transcriptomic changes using context-matched reference signatures. Here we present, a computational framework that estimates thousands of protein activities (currently ~4800) from gene expression at scale, by leveraging context-specific references across major cancer types. In benchmarking analyses, VMPA achieved robust predictive performance (precision-recall AUC > 0.88), inferring activity estimates across diverse protein classes, including kinases, metabolic enzymes, receptors, and transcription factors. Applied to glioblastoma, VMPA tracked protein activity following targeted inhibitor treatments, enabling inference of drug effects on specific protein targets. Furthermore, VMPA identified nine recurrent malignant glioblastoma cell states based on the activity of 2,700 proteins, exposing subpopulations not detectable with gene expression data alone. Finally, we demonstrate the use of VMPA in discovery-driven research by uncovering previously unknown cancer-driver activities in experimental models. In summary, VMPA maps the "active proteome", the ensemble of proteins in their functional states, by inferring protein activity from transcriptomic data, providing a versatile tool for exploring protein function at scale in complex biological systems.

name: Ultrasound-Mediated BBB Opening Promotes Microglial Reprogramming and Enhanced Endothelial Interactions in the Human Peritumoral Brain [scRNA-Seq]
description: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) restricts entry of therapeutics and shapes immune surveillance in the central nervous system, while microglia maintain barrier integrity and coordinate repair. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound with intravenously administered microbubbles (LIPU/MB) transiently opens the BBB in patients, with restoration mostly occurring within about an hour; however, how microglia respond to LIPU/MB during this acute repair window in the human brain remains unknown. We report on intraoperative LIPU/MB studies where the peritumoral brain of glioblastoma patients was biopsied 45 minutes after sonication and analyzed, as part of phase I/II clinical trials (NCT04528680). We integrated single-cell RNA-seq, single-cell ATAC-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and multiplex immunofluorescence. We observe that LIPU/MB modulates perivascular microglia by promoting extension of processes toward the endothelium, inducing pro-inflammatory and chemoattractant transcriptional programs, and remodeling of endothelial–myeloid ligand–receptor communication. We find that microglial reprogramming is accompanied by coordinated changes in chromatin accessibility and heightened activity of the AP-1 transcription factor complex. These results reveal that LIPU/MB-based BBB opening in humans does not merely permit drug passage but reprograms resident myeloid cells to engage the vasculature and amplify innate and adaptive immune pathways, providing a mechanistic basis to leverage immune activation by LIPU/MB with immunotherapies for brain tumors. These findings also warrant consideration in the context of the pathophysiology and therapeutics of CNS diseases where there is acute BBB disruption, or where LIPU/MB is under investigation.

description: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) restricts entry of therapeutics and shapes immune surveillance in the central nervous system, while microglia maintain barrier integrity and coordinate repair. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound with intravenously administered microbubbles (LIPU/MB) transiently opens the BBB in patients, with restoration mostly occurring within about an hour; however, how microglia respond to LIPU/MB during this acute repair window in the human brain remains unknown. We report on intraoperative LIPU/MB studies where the peritumoral brain of glioblastoma patients was biopsied 45 minutes after sonication and analyzed, as part of phase I/II clinical trials (NCT04528680). We integrated single-cell RNA-seq, single-cell ATAC-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and multiplex immunofluorescence. We observe that LIPU/MB modulates perivascular microglia by promoting extension of processes toward the endothelium, inducing pro-inflammatory and chemoattractant transcriptional programs, and remodeling of endothelial–myeloid ligand–receptor communication. We find that microglial reprogramming is accompanied by coordinated changes in chromatin accessibility and heightened activity of the AP-1 transcription factor complex. These results reveal that LIPU/MB-based BBB opening in humans does not merely permit drug passage but reprograms resident myeloid cells to engage the vasculature and amplify innate and adaptive immune pathways, providing a mechanistic basis to leverage immune activation by LIPU/MB with immunotherapies for brain tumors. These findings also warrant consideration in the context of the pathophysiology and therapeutics of CNS diseases where there is acute BBB disruption, or where LIPU/MB is under investigation.

name: Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Unveils Macrophage Involvement in Aortic Valve Stenosis Progression [spatial transcriptome]
description: Introduction: Calcific aortic stenosis (AS) is an age-related progressive disease with increasing global prevalence. Although chronic inflammation is a key factor in its pathogenesis, the detailed immune cell profiles and their interactions with non-immune cells remain poorly understood. This study aimed to characterize the immune cell landscape in calcific AS at a single-cell level and evaluate the potential of anti-inflammatory therapy. Methods: Human aortic valve samples were obtained from four patients with non-calcified aortic regurgitation (AR) and 11 patients with AS undergoing surgical aortic valve replacement. Single-cell 3’ gene expression sequencing (scRNA-seq (3’)) was performed on CD45+ immune cells, while single-cell RNA sequencing Flex (scRNA-seq (Flex)) and bulk RNA sequencing were conducted on unsorted cells. Additionally, an anti-TNFα antibody experiment was performed in a murine AS model induced by aortic valve wire injury. Results: In myeloid cells, LYVE1 resident macrophages were significantly decreased, whereas classical monocytes expressing pro-inflammatory genes and C1Q macrophages were increased in AS valves compared to AR valves. These macrophages exhibited strong interactions with valve interstitial cells, particularly with chondrogenic subtypes expressing COMP and SPARC. Anti-TNFα treatment in the murine model significantly reduced aortic valve calcification without hematopoietic complications. Conclusions: This study is the first to integrate scRNA-seq (3’) and scRNA-seq (Flex) analyses of human aortic valves, revealing single cell-level characteristics of immune cells and their interactions with non-immune cells in calcific AS. These findings suggest that anti-inflammatory therapy could be a therapeutic target for calcific AS.

name: The temporal dynamics of the immune response to neoadjuvant androgen deprivation therapy suggests a window-of-opportunity for checkpoint inhibitor therapy in prostate cancer
description: Background:  Novel therapies to prevent lethal castration resistant prostate cancer in response to standard-of-care androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) are required.  Unfortunately, most prostate cancers are “immune cold” and fail to respond to checkpoint inhibitors (CPIs).  To assess whether ADT induces changes that enable more effective CPI therapy, we examined the tumor immune micro-environment (TiME) following neoadjuvant ADT (nADT).   Methods:  Radical prostatectomy specimens from 43 nADT-treated patients were stratified into three duration of nADT groups and compared to each other and with matched controls.  RNA sequencing and quantitative multispectral immunofluorescence (qmIF) staining were performed to analyze transcriptomic and TiME abundance and cellular spatial relationship differences after nADT.  Results:  Immune and inflammatory pathways, particularly of antigen presentation and adaptive immune response, were increased, most notably in tumors receiving 3-5 months nADT.  qmIF revealed a complex temporal response in the TiME, with a dramatic influx of CTLs and T-helper cells after 3-5 months of nADT.  However, after 6 months nADT, M2-like tumor associated macrophages (TAMs) and Tregs were strikingly increased while CTLs decreased.  Spatially, CTLs and T-helper cells, clustered near tumor cells at 3-5 months nADT, were replaced by M2-TAMs in tumors receiving ≥ 6 months of nADT.  Conclusions: These data reveal the induction of a bi-phasic response in the TiME: robust CTL activation 3-5 months after nADT is initiated, followed by myeloid immunosuppression in tumors receiving prolonged nADT.  This ADT-induced reprogramming of the TiME suggests a critical window of opportunity where short-duration ADT might augment CPI efficacy, converting cold into immunologically responsive tumors.

name: The Reciprocal activation between Leptin Receptor and Hippo/YAP axis in Triple Negative Breast Cancer Development [RNA-Seq Allo-aca]
description: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive breast cancer subtype with limited effective targets. The over-activation of Hippo/YAP axis is often observed in TNBC, but effective therapeutics inhibitors targeting Hippo pathway are still unavailable in clinics. Recently studies implicated the potential link between obesity and increased breast cancer risk, while the adipocytes in mammary gland played important roles in TNBC development but the detailed mechanism is still unclear. In our study, we identified leptin signaling as an important mediator for Hippo/YAP activation and TNBC progression. The paracrine leptin from adipocytes activated leptin receptor (LEPR), which subsequently induced YAP Tyr357 phosphorylation and YAP nuclear trans-location via LEPR/JAK2/SRC axis. Besides, YAP could also bind to the LEPR promoter and enhance its transcription, thereby forming a positive feedback loop in TNBC progression. The paracrine leptin by adipocytes could activate the positive feedback between leptin signaling and Hippo pathway in TNBC development and progression, while pharmaceutical targeting such loop via LEPR inhibition could significantly suppress TNBC carcinogenesis and progression. In collection, our data identified a novel mechanism by the inter-play between leptin system and Hippo/YAP axis in adipocyte-induced breast cancer development and a promising strategy by targeting the membrane receptor LEPR for TNBC therapy.

name: Dimethyl Fumarate Reprograms Liver Cancer Immunity via NF-κB/PD-L1 Suppression and Cuproptosis Induction: A Novel Therapeutic Strategy
description: Background: Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) possesses immunoregulatory and anti-tumor properties, yet its therapeutic potential in liver cancer remains unexplored. This study aimed to investigate DMF’s role in liver cancer immune regulation and elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Methods: Cell viability, proliferation, and cell cycle were assessed using CCK-8, colony formation, and flow cytometry. NF-κB signaling, cuproptosis-related proteins, and PD-L1 were analyzed by Western blot. Aerobic glycolysis and Oxidative phosphorylation were evaluated via ECAR, OCR, lactate production, glucose consumption, and GAPDH activity. PD-L1, HSP70, and DLAT aggregation were quantified by immunofluorescence. The combined anti-tumor efficacy of DMF and cuproptosis induction was validated in a murine liver cancer model. Results: DMF suppressed liver cancer cell viability, clonogenicity, and cell cycle progression while downregulating PD-L1 expression through NF-κB pathway inhibition. It attenuated aerobic glycolysis and promoted cuproptosis. In tumor-immune cell co-cultures, DMF enhanced dendritic cell and natural killer cell function by dual-targeting NF-κB/PD-L1 and inducing cuproptosis. In vivo, DMF combined with Cu-ES increased immune cell infiltration and significantly inhibited tumor progression. Conclusion: DMF combined with cuproptosis induction remodels the tumor immune microenvironment and represents a novel therapeutic strategy to potentiate immunotherapy efficacy in liver cancer.

name: B7-H3 mediates immune escape and metastasis in SCLC through CXCL11/CXCR7/NFIB axis
description: Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an aggressive malignancy that is generally considered an immune desert. The therapeutic impact of immune checkpoint inhibitors in SCLC is modest and confined to a small population of patients. The immune checkpoint protein B7-H3 (also known as CD276) is highly expressed in SCLC; however, its functional contribution to SCLC remains unexplored. Here, to dissect tumor-intrinsic and immunomodulatory functions of B7-H3, we generated a novel genetically engineered mouse (GEM) model Rb1fl/fl; Trp53fl/fl; LSL-MycT58A; Cd276fl/fl (RPMC). Cd276 deletion significantly impaired primary tumor growth, metastatic dissemination, and reprogrammed the SCLC tumor microenvironment by increasing CD8+ T-cell infiltration and decreasing immunosuppressive myeloid populations. Loss of B7-H3 also improved responsiveness to combination therapy (cisplatin and anti-PD-L1) by modulating the anti-tumor immune response. Mechanistically, B7-H3 regulates NFIB through a CXCL11-CXCR7 feed-forward loop. To further evaluate translational implications, we tested a B7-H3 targeted antibody-drug conjugate m276-SL-PBD, which abrogated SCLC in the GEM model. Collectively, our findings establish B7-H3 as a key regulator of SCLC progression, metastatic competence, and immune escape, and highlight B7-H3-directed therapies as promising strategies for this recalcitrant disease.

name: ACSS2 modulates endothelial glycolysis in angiogenesis [Cut&Tag]
description: Endothelial cells (ECs) sustain high glycolytic flux and display remarkable metabolic plasticity. Although the molecular pathways regulating endothelial glycolysis are well characterized, the metabolic mechanisms underlying hypoxia-induced glycolytic activation during angiogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we show that acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 (ACSS2) serves as a critical metabolic modulator, coupling acetate utilization with glycolytic flux to control EC function and angiogenesis. The high level of ACSS2-mediated acetate-to-acetyl-CoA conversion in angiogenic front ECs sustains acetyl-CoA levels, which are essential for EC proliferation and retinal vascularization. Conversely, endothelial-specific Acss2 deletion disrupts pathological angiogenesis and normalizes tumor vasculature. Mechanistically, ACSS2 maintains hypoxia-inducible factor 1α transcriptional activity and stabilizes glucose transporter 1, thereby preserving glycolysis. Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4 knockdown rescues metabolic and functional defects in ACSS2-deficient ECs, revealing acetyl-CoA homeostasis as a lynchpin of hypoxic endothelial metabolism. Collectively, our work establishes ACSS2 as a pivotal regulator of vascular development and proposes targeting acetate metabolism as a strategy to modulate pathological angiogenesis.

name: LRP5-Dependent Transport of Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids Serves as an Immune Checkpoint for Natural Killer Cells
description: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) play a crucial role in tumor development by influencing not only tumor cells but also immune cells within the tumor microenvironment. However, the mechanisms by which PUFAs are transported and function within immune cells to regulate tumor growth remain largely unknown. In this study, we found that LDL Receptor-Related Protein 5 (LRP5) plays an essential role in modulating natural killer (NK) cell antitumor function by facilitating polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) transport through its LDLa domain. The loss of LRP5, particularly its LDLa domain, in NK cells enhances their cytotoxicity and antitumor activity both in vivo and in vitro. However, under PUFA-depleted dietary or culture conditions, wild-type (WT) NK cells also exhibited enhanced cytotoxicity, eliminating the functional difference between WT and LDLa domain–deficient NK cells. Mechanistically, LRP5-mediated PUFA transport suppresses mTORC1 signaling and glycolysis in NK cells, a pathway essential for NK cell cytotoxicity. Thus, our study identifies LRP5 as a critical immune checkpoint that restrains NK cell activity through PUFA transport–dependent suppression of mTORC1 signaling.

name: ISCA1 fuels both oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis to overcome mitotic energy stress
description: The high energy demands associated with mitosis necessitate robust energy production, yet the regulatory mechanisms that mitigate energy stress during this process remain poorly understood. Here, we found that ISCA1 is significantly upregulated in multiple cancer types and is essential for sustaining both oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and glycolysis. Mitochondrial ISCA1 is required for maintaining OXPHOS, while cytoplasmic ISCA1 supports glycolytic function. We observed that ISCA1 expression is markedly elevated in mitotic cells compared to interphase and that it promotes mitotic progression. Moreover, mitotic cells with high ISCA1 levels exhibit increased resistance to apoptosis induced by mitotic arrest or chemotherapeutic drugs. Furthermore, ISCA1 is critical for maintaining energy supply during mitosis and supporting tumor growth. Therefore, our study not only unravels the dual roles of ISCA1 in regulating oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis, but also identifies its essential functions in mitosis and cancer progression, highlighting ISCA1 as a promising therapeutic target for cancer treatment.

name: CASP10-mediated suppression of GSDME-dependent pyroptosis shapes the tumor immune microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma
description: Cancer cells evade immune surveillance by suppressing inflammatory cell death, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Pyroptosis is a lytic form of cell death executed by gasdermin family proteins upon caspase-mediated cleavage. In cancer cells, caspase-3 cleaves GSDME at D270 to release a pore-forming N-terminal fragment that induces pyroptosis. Whether alternative caspase-mediated cleavage of GSDME can suppress pyroptosis has not been explored. Caspase-10 (CASP10) is an initiator caspase that is absent in mice and rats and shares high sequence homology with CASP8. Its substrate specificity and role in cancer cell death remain poorly defined. Here we show that in liver cancer, CASP10 cleaves GSDME at an alternative site (D16), generating a short GSDME-N fragment (amino acids 17–270) that lacks pyroptosis activity. Loss of the N-terminal 1–16 amino acids eliminates the α1 thumb structure required for membrane insertion, abrogating both plasma membrane binding and mitochondrial targeting. Furthermore, short GSDME-N associates with canonical GSDME-N and blocks its oligomerization, thereby suppressing pyroptosis. In vivo experiments and single-cell transcriptomic analysis of human liver cancer demonstrate that CASP10 promotes immune evasion and is associated with invasive metastatic progression. Targeting CASP10 with antisense oligonucleotides restores pyroptosis and suppresses tumor growth. These findings reveal CASP10-mediated alternative cleavage of GSDME as a pyroptosis-suppressive mechanism in cancer, and identify CASP10 as a therapeutic target and a biomarker of metastatic progression in liver cancer.

name: Selective expansion of neoantigen-specific peripheral blood lymphocytes through antigen presenting cell-T cell conjugate isolation
description: Neoantigen-specific peripheral blood lymphocytes (NeoPBL) are the circulating counterparts of neoantigen-specific tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL). A recent study showed NeoPBL exist in a less differentiated state in vivo than TIL, which, along with their non-invasive potential, makes them attractive for cell therapy. However, NeoPBL circulate at ultra-low frequencies, usually less than 0.005%, posing a major translational barrier for their clinical use. Here we use NeoSelect, a peptide-based cyclic enrichment and expansion strategy that leverages magnetic selection of antigen-presenting cell-NeoPBL conjugates ex vivo to increase the frequency of NeoPBL by thousands of folds over 28 days while also achieving large-scale expansion. We then evaluated expanded cells using functional, transcriptomic and epigenetic profiling. Most NeoPBL clonotypes amplified by NeoSelect are detectable as exhausted TIL in vivo. In addition, neoantigen-specific TIL that failed to expand during ex vivo culture could be recovered as NeoPBL. Transcriptional and epigenetic analyses reveal that ex vivo NeoPBL have distinct transcriptional and epigenetic programs compared to TIL, and retain expression of and chromatin accessibility at genes associated with stemness (TCF7, KLF2) and costimulation (CD28, CD40LG). NeoPBL encompass physiologically relevant anti-tumor clonotypes, can be rapidly expanded to clinically useful numbers and frequencies ex vivo, and can be used to expand the targetable neoantigen repertoire. By combining broad potential applicability and minimal invasiveness, these results position NeoPBL as a clinically streamlined and biologically distinct autologous cell platform that may be useful for adoptive cell transfer

name: Cellular and Molecular changes underpinning the formation of Intimal Hyperplasia in a model of static Human Saphenous Vein Ex Vivo Culture
description: Intimal hyperplasia (IH) significantly limits the long-term patency of saphenous vein grafts following bypass surgery, with no with no widely accepted human models that fully captures its complex pathogenesis. Although animal models, primarily murine systems, have provided mechanistic insights into IH, limitations persist in translating these findings to human pathophysiology. Human saphenous vein segments obtained from patients who underwent lower limb bypass surgery were cultured ex vivo for 7 days under static conditions. Bulk RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics (GeoMx) were employed to characterize the localized transcriptional alterations. Cultured vein segments developed characteristic features of IH, including marked endothelial dysfunction, increased vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC) apoptosis and proliferation, extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling and neointima formation. Spatial transcriptomics revealed localized VSMC dedifferentiation and activation of inflammatory, oxidative stress, and ECM remodelling pathways. We further observed upregulation of osteogenic markers Sox9 and RunX2, and RunX2 inhibition limited IH.

name: Type II IL-4 receptor complex drives mesenchymal fibroblast activation in keloids via STAT6 signaling
description: Keloids result from aberrant wound healing characterized by excessive collagen and mesenchymal-related protein production. The type II IL-4 receptor complex, composed of IL-4Rα and IL-13Rα1, is implicated in keloid pathogenesis but remains underexplored. To address this, we applied single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) to healthy normal skin, adjacent normal skin, active keloids, and regressed keloids. Integrated scRNA-seq and ST analyses identified IL4R+/IL13RA1+/POSTN+ fibroblasts with combined reticular and mesenchymal phenotypes that were enriched in fibrotic regions of keloids. Immunofluorescence studies confirmed co-localization of IL4R, IL13RA1, and POSTN proteins in keloid tissue. Elevated mRNA levels of IL4R, IL13RA1, COL1A1, FN1, and POSTN were found in both keloid tissue and fibroblasts compared to normal skin. Furthermore, silencing IL13RA1 or IL4R using siRNA in keloid fibroblasts (KFs) resulted in reduced expression of COL1A1, FN1, and POSTN. Lastly, inhibiting type II receptor signaling with dupilumab, an anti-IL4R monoclonal antibody, suppressed IL-13-induced COL1A1, FN1, and POSTN protein expression in KF and collagen deposition in keloid explants. In conclusion, our in vitro and ex vivo findings suggest that inhibition of type II IL-4 receptor signaling with dupilumab may reduce mesenchymal protein expression and collagen deposition, warranting further investigation of this pathway in keloid disease.

name: In situ generation of immunostimulatory bacterial lysates by tumor-targeted self-destructive bacteria for cancer therapy
description: Bacteriotherapy has attracted considerable interest for cancer treatment due to the natural tumor tropism of bacteria. However, safety concerns associated with live bacterial administration limit its clinical translation. Here, we propose a lysate-based therapeutic strategy that preserves bacterial immunostimulatory capacity while minimizing risks linked to bacterial proliferation. Systematic evaluation of multiple bacterial lysates identified Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) lysate as a potent inducer of antitumor immunity, exhibiting both direct cytotoxicity toward tumor cells via apoptosis and necrosis and strong immune activation capacity. Based on this finding, we engineered a tumor-responsive bacterial platform, CAP-MM@EcN, by conjugating the broad-spectrum antibiotic chloramphenicol (CAP) onto macrophage membrane-camouflaged EcN via a ROS/GSH dual-responsive linker. The macrophage membrane coating enhances systemic biocompatibility and tumor accumulation, while elevated redox signals within the tumor microenvironment trigger localized antibiotic release, inducing bacterial self-lysis and simultaneous eradication of endogenous intratumoral bacteria, thereby enabling in situ generation of immunogenic bacterial lysates. This self-destructive bacterial activation remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by promoting M1 macrophage polarization, dendritic cell maturation, and cytotoxic T cell activation. In multiple murine tumor models, CAP-MM@EcN elicited robust antitumor responses, with tumor inhibition rates reaching 87.5%, demonstrating a safe and effective strategy for bacteria-mediated cancer immunotherapy.

name: Activation of the NF-κB/ALDH1A1 Signaling Promotes Non-Mutational Resistance to EGFR-TKIs in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
description: Acquired resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) remains a major clinical challenge in the treatment of EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study established TKI-resistant variants by integrating cell lines, lung cancer organoids (LCOs), and in vivo models, revealing the pivotal role of the NF-κB/ALDH1A1 signaling in mediating non-mutational TKI resistance. Resistant cells exhibited elevated RELA phosphorylation, enhanced ALDH1A1 expression and enzymatic activity, and stem-like properties. Mechanistically, NF-κB activation occurred as an early response to TKI exposure and promoted ALDH1A1 transcription via RELA. In turn, ALDH1A1 contributed to the sustained activation of NF-κB signaling, forming a self-reinforcing positive feedback loop.. Genetic ALDH1A1 or RELA silencing reversed the resistant phenotype. Pharmacologically, treatment with an EGFR-TKI and the ALDH1A1 inhibitor disulfiram or the NF-κB-targeting agent EGCG synergistically restored the antitumor efficacy of TKIs both in vitro and in vivo. These findings establish the NF-κB/ALDH1A1 signaling as a key non-genetic mechanism of acquired EGFR-TKI resistance and provide a rational combination strategy to overcome it.

name: Chromatin-associated miRNAs in PANC-1 cells: strong chromatin abundance of miR-21 and candidates with RNA-DNA triplex-forming potential
description: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are best known for their role in post-transcriptional gene regulation in the cytoplasm. However, a subset of miRNAs has been detected in the nucleus, suggesting additional regulatory functions. Here, we systematically characterize chromatin-associated small non-coding RNAs in the human pancreatic cancer cell line PANC-1. Using chromatin RNA immunoprecipitation coupled with small RNA sequencing, we show that the chromatin-associated small RNA population differs markedly from the bulk nuclear RNA pool and is strongly enriched in miRNAs. Among these, miR-21 represents the most abundant chromatin-associated species. In parallel, sequence analyses further revealed that a distinct subset of chromatin-associated miRNAs fulfills sequence requirements compatible with RNA–DNA triplex formation at genomic regulatory regions. Gel-shift assays demonstrate that Argonaute2 (Ago2) can interact with triple-helical structures in vitro, providing biochemical support for Ago2 recognition of such triplex substrates. Evolutionary analyses indicate that triplex-forming chromatin-associated miRNAs show a restricted phyletic distribution, with the full complement observed only in anthropoid primates, in contrast to the much broader conservation of non-triplex-forming miRNAs. Together, our results define a chromatin-associated miRNA landscape in PANC-1 cells, highlight miR-21 as the most abundant chromatin-associated miRNA, and identify candidate triplex-forming miRNAs and Ago2-triplex interactions that outline a testable hypothesis for an additional mode of miRNA-chromatin communication.
assay_text: Non-coding RNA profiling by high throughput sequencing

name: Localized fever mimicry within lymph node potentiates cancer vaccine efficacy
description: The development of cancer vaccines is hampered by low immunogenicity and weak immune response in patients. Inspired by fever and thermal regulation of immunity, we constructed photothermal gold nanoparticles-based cancer vaccines to “heat” draining lymph nodes to 39-40°C under near-infrared laser irradiation.Remarkably, the local hyperthermia generated in lymph nodes was demonstrated to facilitate antigen presentation of dendritic cells, selectively promote T helper 17 (Th17) cell differentiation, and elicit potent tumor antigen-specific CD8+ T cell response while reducing immunosuppressive regulatory T cells (Treg) expansion, resulting in superior therapeutic efficacy in murine melanoma lung metastasis model and subcutaneous model.

name: Vascular smooth muscle cell abundance is a hallmark of Castleman Disease
description: Castleman Disease (CD) is a poorly understood inflammatory disorder characterized by enlarged lymph nodes with distinctive histologic features. Its opaque pathophysiology delays diagnoses and limits treatments, leading to additional morbidity and mortality. Since lymph nodes are the key lesional tissue for the disease, we sought to better understand the molecular and cellular underpinnings of CD lymph nodes using single cell and spatial transcriptomics. We found pronounced alterations in cell composition and dysregulation of distinct molecular pathways in non-hematopoietic stromal cells in lymph nodes from the unicentric form of CD. In contrast, hematopoietic cells in CD lymph nodes showed only few compositional or expression changes when compared to enlarged lymph nodes with non-specific inflammation. The elevated abundance of vascular smooth muscle cells, a subset of lymph node stromal cells, in unicentric CD lymph nodes and broadly increased stromal cell activity signified CD lymph nodes. In particular, immunohistochemical staining for the vascular smooth muscle cell marker CD146 (Melanoma Cell Adhesion Molecule, MCAM) served as reliable discriminator of unicentric CD lymph nodes from related lymphadenopathies. In sum, single cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses of CD lymph nodes facilitate the identification of CD-specific molecular and cellular features to guide diagnosis and patient stratification.

name: The Reciprocal activation between Leptin Receptor and Hippo/YAP axis in Triple Negative Breast Cancer Development
description: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive breast cancer subtype with limited effective targets. The over-activation of Hippo/YAP axis is often observed in TNBC, but effective therapeutics inhibitors targeting Hippo pathway are still unavailable in clinics. Recently studies implicated the potential link between obesity and increased breast cancer risk, while the adipocytes in mammary gland played important roles in TNBC development but the detailed mechanism is still unclear. In our study, we identified leptin signaling as an important mediator for Hippo/YAP activation and TNBC progression. The paracrine leptin from adipocytes activated leptin receptor (LEPR), which subsequently induced YAP Tyr357 phosphorylation and YAP nuclear trans-location via LEPR/JAK2/SRC axis. Besides, YAP could also bind to the LEPR promoter and enhance its transcription, thereby forming a positive feedback loop in TNBC progression. The paracrine leptin by adipocytes could activate the positive feedback between leptin signaling and Hippo pathway in TNBC development and progression, while pharmaceutical targeting such loop via LEPR inhibition could significantly suppress TNBC carcinogenesis and progression. In collection, our data identified a novel mechanism by the inter-play between leptin system and Hippo/YAP axis in adipocyte-induced breast cancer development and a promising strategy by targeting the membrane receptor LEPR for TNBC therapy.

name: TNFα Priming of Human Pericytes Enhances TGFβ1-Smad Signaling and Microvascular Fibrotic Activation Via and Increase in TGFβRII Activity
description: Effective anti-fibrotic treatments remain elusive, as current drugs do not reverse fibrotic progression. A deeper understanding of how understudied contributor cells, such as pericytes, intersect with inflammatory and fibrotic cues is needed to uncover mechanisms driving fibrosis. We hypothesize that pro-inflammatory tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) can modulate transforming growth factor- β1 (TGFβ1) signaling in a time dependent manner in human pericytes via an increase in TGFβRII activity. Pericytes were subject to either Priming (4 hours of TNFα treatment followed by TGFβ1 treatment) or Coactivation (TNFα and TGFβ1 simultaneous treatment) to assess the role of TNFα activity on TGFβ1, resulting in distinct genetic profiles and ultimately differences in downstream pSmad2 activation, collagen deposition, MMP secretion and cellular contraction. Altogether, these findings provide evidence that the timing of TNFα exposure shapes its influence on TGFβ1-mediated fibrotic signaling in pericytes, at times exacerbating and at times attenuating pericyte fibrotic responses.

name: Spatially-resolved simultaneous mapping of drug-genome and histone-DNA interactions in tissue sections with EPIC-map
description: We developed EPIC-map that overcomes existing limitations in drug map by simultaneously maps genome-wide small-molecule binding and histone modifications on the same tissue section. To validate the data quality of EPIC-map, we first captured and analyzed drug-binding sites in colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) tissues. Results demonstrated that EPIC-map successfully identified distinct tumor subpopulations and their differential binding sites for different drugs at both 50 um and 20 um resolutions, confirming its robustness in technical reproducibility and data quality. Subsequent multi-modal co-profiling further verified that Epic-map maintains high data quality without compromising the performance of either individual modality. Applied to mouse and human KRAS-driven colorectal cancer samples, EPIC-map enabled characterization of the tumor microenvironment and uncovered chromatin state dependent drug interactions alongside heterogeneous drug engagement across tumor subregions. Furthermore, EPIC-map delineated the molecular mechanisms underlying KRAS inhibitor resistance, guiding the design of combined chemotherapy and epigenetic drugs to eradicate cancer cells by synergistically abolishing epithelial–mesenchymal transition and intratumoral heterogeneity.

name: MICAL2 as a Key Effector of β-Catenin Signaling Driving Melanoma Progression and Therapeutic Resistance
description: β-catenin plays a pivotal role in oncogenesis through its involvement in cell-cell adhesion, Wnt signaling, and transcriptional regulation. Dysregulation of β-catenin contributes to tumorigenesis by promoting proliferation, bypassing senescence, and enhancing migration and invasion. In melanoma, however, its role has been controversial, with studies reporting conflicting effects on proliferation, metastasis, and patient survival. Here, we demonstrate that activation of β-catenin is associated with a poor prognosis in melanoma. This conclusion is based on an immunohistochemical analysis of a cohort of 157 patients and the identification of a genetic signature for melanoma associated with β-catenin activation. This signature includes known targets such as APCDD1 and AXIN2, as well as previously unknown targets like MICAL2 and SLC1A5. Notably, MICAL2 emerged as a key regulator of the invasive phenotype, with high expression levels correlating with adverse outcomes. Functional studies confirmed that MICAL2 is transcriptionally regulated by β-catenin. Oncogenic β-catenin expression in Nras and Braf mouse models further validated the conserved regulation of MICAL2, linking it to melanoma initiation and metastasis. Moreover, MICAL2 expression is enriched in melanoma cells resistant to BRAF inhibitors, and MICAL2 downregulation restores therapeutic sensitivity. These findings highlight MICAL2 as a central effector of β-catenin signaling and a mediator of melanoma progression and resistance. Given the therapeutic challenges of directly targeting β-catenin, the enzymatic activity of MICAL2 presents a promising alternative strategy. Targeting MICAL2 could therefore represent an innovative approach to improve clinical outcomes in melanoma patients with β-catenin–driven disease.

name: Nonopore sequencing of circRNAs and G3BP2-RIP sequencing in HCC827 cells
description: Acquired resistance to third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as almonertinib presents a major clinical challenge in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are generated via back-splicing, and are versatile players in cancer biology. By using long-read nanopore sequencing, we profiled full-length circRNAs in almonertinib-resistant NSCLC cells and identified widespread alternative back-splicing (ABS) events in circRNAs. Among them, exon 3 of the PUM1 gene was a significantly regulated ABS exon, and led to the generation of most upregulated circRNA isoform of circPUM1(2-3) compared to circPUM1(2) in the resistant cells. Functional studies revealed that circPUM1(2-3) promoted cell viability and suppressed apoptosis by binding to the RNA-binding protein G3BP2 via its exon 3 sequences. This interaction competitively disrupted the G3BP2 binding to PSMA6 mRNA, which then increased the PSMA6 mRNA and protein levels, and led to the activation of MAPK/ERK pathway to promote cell survival.

name: UTY coordinates with UTX to repress NK cell development and maturation in males
description: Natural killer (NK) cells are pivotal innate lymphoid cells in anti-tumor immunity. However, the contribution of the Y chromosome-encoded epigenetic regulator UTY (also known as KDM6C) to male NK cell development and effector function remains poorly characterized. Here, we demonstrated that conditional deletion of UTY in NK cells (Ncr1-iCre) in male mice led to a statistically significant but modest increase in total NK cell numbers (p < 0.05) and an elevated frequency of terminally differentiated CD27−CD11b+ subset in the spleen. Strikingly, UTY-deficient NK cells displayed impaired cytotoxic function, with significantly reduced granzyme B expression (p < 0.05) and attenuated control of B16F10 melanoma pulmonary metastases in vivo (p < 0.05). Importantly, combined UTX-UTY deficiency exacerbated these phenotypes, causing further decline in NK cell abundance, CD27+CD11b+ subset proportions, and granzyme B expression level compared with UTX single knockout in male mice. RNA-sequencing combined with qRT-PCR validation uncovered significant downregulation of key genes involved in NK cell maturation (Cd27), cytotoxicity (Gzmb), survival (Bax, Casp3) and transcriptional regulation (Socs3, Tcf7) in UTY-deficient NK cells. Notably, dual UTX-UTY depletion synergistically repressed Casp3 expression, potentially contributing to the altered NK cell abundance (p < 0.05). These findings establish UTY as a sex-specific epigenetic modulator that restricts NK cell maturation while licensing cytotoxic function. Our data further reveal a cooperative role for UTX and UTY in orchestrating NK cell development via transcriptional regulation.
